newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Softer crown keeps Swedish Riksbank from rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: Softer crown keeps Swedish Riksbank from rate cuts.

text.p: Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, is anxious to continue cutting interest rates but is held back by a currency weakened by signals the government is loosening its grip on fiscal policy, analysts said on Thursday.
The Riksbank's governor and deputy governor in separate speeches this week said the softening Swedish crown was not affecting the country's economic fundamentals.
Deputy governor Lars Heikensten told a meeting on Wednesday that the weaker crown has contributed to the bank not cutting its key interest rate, the repo rate, since December 17.

The bank had, until then, been cutting the rate frequently with 25 cuts from early 1996 when the repo rate was 8.91 percent. It currently stands at 4.10 percent while deposit and lending rates are 3.75 percent and 5.25 percent respectively.
"We have seen certain signs that economic trends have become marginally weaker," Heikensten said.
"On the other hand we have the crown softening. Foreign exchange rates are an important factor, and it is one of the factors that changes the fastest."
Riksbank governor Urban Backstrom indicated at a London seminar on Tuesday that there was room for a crown rebound.

"The exchange rate has become weaker than what was assumed in the (Riksbank's) latest inflation report and the current foreign exchange rate level does not reflect fundamental trends in the economy," Backstrom said.
Neither Backstrom nor Heikensten saw any reason to change the conclusions of the bank's latest, quarterly inflation report, which was released on December 1996.

The recent crown softening followed comments by Prime Minister Goran Persson and Finance Minister Erik Asbrink that the government would spend 10 billion crowns ($1.4 billion) of expected coming budget surpluses on health care, elderly care, child care and schools as of 1998.
Market turmoil was fuelled by Asbrink on Wednesday when he clarified that the government would spend the 10 billion crowns in 1998 even if state finances were weaker than expected.
Since January 22 when Persson started talking about spending some of the coming budget surpluses instead of paying off state debt, the crown has dropped to 4.4110 against the mark from 4.3670.
The nine-year bond yield has surged to 6.79 percent from 6.59 percent.
Economists are mainly worried that the government will abandon its strict fiscal policies and instead start spending to win votes in the general elections due September 1998.

"As the government currently holds 30 percent of votes (according to polls), there is a significant risk that more measures will be initiated during the period before the election," said James McKay, economist at U.S. investment bank PaineWebber.
Economists also find it risky to give promises based on expected budget surpluses, which are not certain to happen.
Several economists believe the negative effects of Persson's move will hover in the market for several months.

"I do not see any room for any immediate crown strengthening, rather a further weakening of the crown. There is a risk that there will be turmoil until the budget proposal in April," an economist said.
